:::{#thm-exp-above-tangent}
#### The exponential function lies above its tangent line at zero

For every [real](https://morrison-lab.github.io/mcs/number-systems.html#def-real-numbers) $x$,

$$\expf{x} \ge 1 + x,$$

with equality exactly when $x = 0$.

:::

::: proof

Let $g(x) \eqdef \expf{x} - 1 - x$.
The [exponential function](algebra.qmd#def-exponential-function) has [second derivative](calculus-derivatives.qmd#def-second-derivative) $\expf{x} > 0$ at every $x$,
so it is [convex](algebra.qmd#def-convex-function) by @thm-convex-hessian.
The function $g$ differs from it by a [linear function](algebra.qmd#def-linear-function),
so $g$ is convex too.
The [derivative](calculus-derivatives.qmd#def-derivative) of $g$ is $\dif{g(x)}{x} = \expf{x} - 1$,
which is $0$ at $x = 0$.
By @cor-convex-stationary, $0$ is a [global minimizer](algebra.qmd#def-global-minimizer) of $g$,
and $g(0) = 0$,
so $g(x) \ge 0$ for every $x$.

Suppose $g(x) = 0$ for some $x$.
Then $x$ is also a global minimizer of $g$,
and so a [local minimizer](algebra.qmd#def-local-minimizer).
[Fermat's theorem](optimization-critical-points.qmd#thm-fermat) gives $\dif{g(x)}{x} = \expf{x} - 1 = 0$.
Then $\expf{x} = 1 = \expf{0}$,
which gives $x = 0$
because the exponential function is injective.

:::
